name: Hydroquinone

lead: Hydroquinone is a long-established skin-lightening agent used for melasma, sun spots and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. It has been regarded as the reference standard among topical depigmenting treatments, typically as a prescription product or compounded formulation.
Regulation differs by country, with some regions restricting or banning cosmetic use and others permitting it under prescription control.

paras: Hydroquinone inhibits tyrosinase, the enzyme that drives melanin synthesis, and also impairs melanosome formation and promotes melanocyte degradation, resulting in reduced pigment production.

Common effects are irritation and contact dermatitis. Prolonged or high-concentration use, especially of unregulated products, can cause exogenous ochronosis, a hard-to-treat blue-black discoloration, and paradoxical darkening. Continuous use is usually limited to short courses under supervision. Safety questions about systemic exposure have led to restrictions in several jurisdictions.

lead: Hydroquinone (benzene-1,4-diol) is an aromatic compound and a phenol. Industrially it is best known as a photographic developing agent and polymerization inhibitor; in dermatology it is applied topically as a skin-lightening agent for melasma, solar lentigines (sun spots) and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, alone or in combination creams.[1][2] The name was coined by Friedrich Wohler in 1843.[1]

A number of reviews describe it as the long-standing reference treatment for hyperpigmentation: a 2022 systematic review calls topical hydroquinone the gold standard in melasma, and a 2020 evidence-based review found a triple combination cream (hydroquinone, tretinoin and a corticosteroid) and hydroquinone alone to be the most effective melasma treatments among those examined.[3][4] Newer agents such as tranexamic acid and thiamidol have been compared against it in randomized trials with mixed relative results.[2][5][6]

Its regulation is contested and varies by country. Reviews report restrictions or bans on cosmetic use in the European Union, Japan and Australia, and Wikipedia reports that the US FDA withdrew over-the-counter hydroquinone in 2020 on the grounds that carcinogenicity could not be ruled out, while prescription products remain available; documented adverse effects include contact dermatitis and, with chronic use, exogenous ochronosis.[1][2]
infobox: 2 to 4 percent (review figure); up to 5 percent in some use
Prescription-only or restricted in many regions; banned for cosmetic use in some (EU, Japan, Australia per a review); US OTC use withdrawn

paras: Hydroquinone is used to lighten dark patches from melasma, sun-induced lentigines and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, and appears in photoaging regimens alongside botanicals and peptides in cosmeceutical reviews.[2][7][8] It is also found in combination products, such as the triple combination with tretinoin and a corticosteroid, and a 1975 trial combined 5 percent hydroquinone, 0.1 percent tretinoin and 0.1 percent dexamethasone for melasma and related pigmentation.[1][4]

Outside medicine, hydroquinone is a main component of black-and-white photographic developers, a polymerization inhibitor and an antioxidant intermediate.[1] A beetle species, the bombardier beetle, uses hydroquinone and hydrogen peroxide in its defensive spray, a topic that appears in unrelated T Nation evolution threads.[1][9][10]

Hydroquinone has been reported to improve melasma. A narrative review cites a 2020 report of 96 percent improvement with 3 percent hydroquinone twice daily plus sunscreen versus 81 percent with hydroquinone alone, and a 30-person study in which 2 percent hydroquinone-cyclodextrin lightened solar lentigines over two months; the review itself notes its evidence base is small studies, and that effects typically appear after about 5 to 7 weeks with courses of at least three months in melasma.[2]

Comparator trials give mixed relative results. In the review's summary, 4 percent hydroquinone acted faster than kojic acid, while 3 percent tranexamic acid produced a greater reduction in MASI and melanin index than 4 percent hydroquinone in one trial, and 0.2 percent thiamidol outperformed 2 percent hydroquinone in another.[2] Other randomized trials have compared thiamidol with 4 percent hydroquinone in 50 women,[5] tranexamic acid cream with hydroquinone in a split-face design,[6] and tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams with hydroquinone.[11] A systematic review states that the superiority of microneedling and peels to hydroquinone remains to be established and that recurrence rates remain high in all treatment groups.[3]

Human trials include comparisons with thiamidol (n=50),[5] with 3 percent tranexamic acid in a double-blind split-face trial,[6] with niosomal and conventional tranexamic acid/niacinamide creams,[11] with kojic acid and azelaic acid in melasma,[2][12] and a registered trial against miconazole (n=60),[13] a 4 percent cream phase 3 study (n=17),[14] hexyresorcinol versus hydroquinone for photoaging (n=32),[15] and several comparisons against other formulas and oils.[16][17]

Systematic and consensus reviews include a review of 113 controlled studies with 6,897 participants (2020),[4] a 2022 systematic review,[3] a 2024 update on new and existing melasma treatments,[18] and a 2026 Pigmentary Disorders Society Delphi consensus with 38 dermatologists from 11 countries.[19]

Reviews list allergic or irritant contact dermatitis, hypopigmentation and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation as short-term effects. Exogenous ochronosis, a blue-black or gray-brown pigmentation of sun-exposed skin, is described as the most frequent effect of chronic use and largely permanent, although dermabrasion and laser treatment have helped in some cases.[2][20] Less common reports include trimethylaminuria, nail hyperpigmentation, reduced skin elasticity, impaired wound healing and peripheral neuropathy.[2]

On systemic safety, the review states that hydroquinone is absorbed through skin, that rodent studies show DNA damage and a few human cases of squamous cell carcinoma are on record, and that there is insufficient evidence that topical use causes cancer in humans; it advises pregnant or breastfeeding individuals to limit exposure.[2] Wikipedia reports that the FDA concluded in its regulatory review that carcinogenic potential could not be excluded, citing rodent tumour findings and absorption in humans.[1]

Hydroquinone is oxidized by tyrosinase in preference to tyrosine, lowering melanin formation. The review also describes disruption of the melanocyte cytoskeleton and melanosome transport and inhibition of DNA and RNA synthesis, and suggests this disruption may contribute more than tyrosinase inhibition; it also scavenges free radicals.[2]

Hydroquinone is a white granular solid with two hydroxyl groups para to each other on a benzene ring. It is made industrially from 1,4-diisopropylbenzene via a cumene-like process or by hydroxylating phenol, and it can be reversibly oxidised to benzoquinone.[1]

Its skin-lightening effect was first reported in 1936; in the 1950s it was used in a sunscreen formulation in the southern United States, where lightening was noticed as a side effect; it was trialed for hyperpigmentation in 1961.[1] Wikipedia reports that the FDA classified it as generally recognized as safe and effective in 1982, revoked its approval and proposed an over-the-counter ban in 2006, and banned it in 2020 as part of an over-the-counter drug reform.[1]

Wikipedia states it is prescription-only in EU member states under a 1976 cosmetics directive, whereas a 2023 review states that its use is banned in the EU, Japan and Australia; in the US over-the-counter products are not FDA-approved and the compound is available as a prescription pharmaceutical.[1][2] In 2023 it was the 274th most prescribed medication in the US, with over 800,000 prescriptions.[1]

T Nation users mention it in small numbers: one poster used a hydroquinone product for about four months to even skin tone, and another used it with tretinoin and pulsed dye laser on steroid-related acne scars.[21][22]

lore.intro: Hydroquinone appears only occasionally in the forum material reviewed, as a pigment-evening ingredient in skin-care and acne-scar threads.[21][22]
